nameStory: The name 'pigweed' comes from its historical use as food for pigs, though the 'smooth' part of its name refers to its relatively hairless stems and leaves. The scientific name 'hybridus' hints at its tendency to cross-pollinate with other amaranths, creating natural hybrids that can make identification tricky.
description: Smooth pigweed is a tall, upright annual weed that can grow 3-6 feet high in a single growing season. It has a sturdy, branching stem topped with dense, greenish flower spikes that look almost fuzzy from a distance. The leaves are oval-shaped with pointed tips, and the whole plant has a somewhat coarse, weedy appearance that you'll often find growing in disturbed soil.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, greenish spikes at the top of the plant that feel rough and bristly to the touch, made up of tiny flowers packed tightly together

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with pointed tips, arranged alternately on the stem, feeling smooth to slightly rough but not fuzzy or hairy

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright plant that can tower over other weeds, with multiple branches near the top creating a somewhat pyramid shape

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, shiny black seeds that fall easily from the flower spikes when mature, often creating small piles beneath the plant

habitat: You'll find smooth pigweed thriving in disturbed soils like gardens, farm fields, roadsides, and vacant lots throughout New England. It loves rich, nitrogen-rich soil and full sun, often appearing as one of the first weeds to colonize freshly turned earth or compost piles.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with oval leaves, easily overlooked among other emerging weeds.
seasonality.summer: Plants shoot up rapidly, developing their characteristic tall stems and dense flower spikes that bloom from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes turn brown and release masses of tiny black seeds, while the whole plant begins to die back with the first frosts.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stems may persist, but the annual plant has died completely, leaving only seeds in the soil for next year.

funFact: A single smooth pigweed plant can produce up to 100,000 seeds in one season, and those seeds can remain viable in the soil for decades, waiting for the right conditions to sprout!
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with redroot amaranth, but smooth pigweed has smoother leaves and stems, while redroot amaranth feels more rough and hairy. Memory trick: 'smooth' pigweed actually feels smoother to the touch than its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'weed,' smooth pigweed is actually edible and nutritious - the young leaves can be cooked like spinach, and the seeds were once ground into flour by Native Americans. Many gardeners don't realize they're pulling up a perfectly good food plant!
compareHints: Compared to redroot amaranth, smooth pigweed has less hairy stems and leaves, and its flower spikes tend to be more upright rather than drooping. Unlike spiny amaranth, it has no sharp spines on its stems, making it much safer to handle with bare hands.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England amaranths, redroot is distinguished by its reddish taproot and compact, bristly flower clusters.
Unlike the weedy Redroot Amaranth found in gardens and fields, Tidalmarsh Amaranth is strictly a coastal specialist that grows much taller and in dense colonies.

Purple amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives by its distinctly prostrate, mat-forming growth habit - while redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed grow upright like small bushes, purple amaranth sprawls along the ground.
Among its amaranth relatives, red amaranth stands out for its particularly robust, upright growth and thick, erect flower spikes.
Love-lies-bleeding stands out dramatically from its wild amaranth relatives in New England because of its long, pendulous flower clusters - all the others have upright, spike-like flower heads.
Among the New England amaranths, rough-fruit amaranth stands out for its preference for wetter habitats and its distinctively bumpy seeds.
Among New England's amaranths, green amaranth is unique for maintaining its green color throughout the season - most others develop reddish or purplish tones in stems, roots, or flower clusters.
Among New England's amaranths, spiny amaranth is the only one with actual spines - species like redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed may have bristly flowers but lack the sharp spines at leaf bases.
Palmer's Amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives because it's 'dioecious' - meaning individual plants are either male or female, not both like most other amaranths.
Powell's amaranth differs from redroot amaranth by lacking the red-tinged roots and having less hairy leaves.
Unlike its weedy cousins like Redroot Amaranth that grow tall and upright in disturbed soils, Seabeach Amaranth stays flat against the sand and has much thicker, more succulent leaves and stems.
